notes.t: timeout-minutes — kill a stuck job after 15 min, not 6 h
continue-on-error — lint may fail without failing the job
if: failure() — runs only when something broke
if: always() — cleanup, pass or fail

captions: Part four. Runners and jobs.
Where does your code actually run, and how do
jobs work together?
The easy option is a GitHub-hosted runner.

You write runs-on ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, or
macos-latest, and GitHub

hands you a fresh virtual machine, preloaded with
common
tools.

There are Arm runners, larger machines with more
cores,
and even GPU runners.
The key word is ephemeral. Every job gets a
clean machine, and it's wiped when the job ends.

Nothing leaks between runs. That's why builds are
reproducible
— and why you'll want caching, which we'll see
later.
A single job on a hosted runner can run
for up to six hours.
The other option is a self-hosted runner: your own
machine, registered with GitHub.
A small agent on it asks GitHub for work,
runs the job, and reports back.
Why do this? Special hardware. Access to a private

network. Or heavy workloads where your own machines
are
cheaper.
At scale, teams run the Actions Runner Controller on

Kubernetes. It watches the queue and scales runner
pods
up and down automatically.

The trade-off: you now own patching, security and
cleanup.

And never attach self-hosted runners to public
repositories —
a stranger's pull request could run code on your
machine.
A workflow can hold many jobs, and by default
they all start at once, in parallel.
To order them, use needs. Here, unit tests and

end-to-end tests both need build. Deploy needs every
check.
GitHub turns that into a graph, and starts each
job the moment its needs are done.

Watch the timeline. Run one after another, these
jobs
take eleven minutes. Run as a graph, just six.
And if a job fails, everything that needs it
is skipped. A broken build never reaches deploy.
Need to test on several platforms? Don't copy the
job — use a matrix.

Give it lists: three operating systems, and three
Node
versions.

GitHub multiplies them out: three times three, nine
jobs,
all in parallel.

exclude removes combinations you don't need. include
adds special
ones. Here we drop one and add one —
still nine.
By default, fail-fast is on: if one job fails,
GitHub cancels the rest to save time. Turn it
off when you want the full picture.
One matrix can generate up to two hundred and
fifty six jobs.
Jobs often need a real database to test against.
That's what service containers are for.
Under services, you name a container — say Postgres
— with its image, a password and a health
check.
GitHub starts it next to your job, waits until
it's healthy, and your tests connect to it.
When the job ends, it's thrown away. Every run
gets a clean database.
You can even run the whole job inside a

container, with the container key. Same idea: you
choose
the exact environment.
Real pipelines also need to control failure.

First, timeout minutes. A hung test could otherwise
burn
up to six hours. Set a sensible limit, like
fifteen minutes.
Next, continue on error. Here, lint may fail without
failing the whole job — useful for a check
you're still rolling out.
Normally, a failed step stops the job. But a
step with if failure runs only when something broke
— perfect for alerting the team.
And if always runs no matter what, so the
cleanup happens every single time.
